title: Cold Iron at the Fords
text: With the toll-brigands broken and the river crossings cleared, flat-bottomed barges finally resumed hauling timber and salted pike into Thornwick. Yet the victory brought no royal relief—only tax-assessors arriving under heavy escort to audit the salvaged granaries. Along Alder Bridge, blacksmiths melted down captured spearheads into plowshares and wagon-tires while widows patched the palisades before autumn rains swelled the banks once more. The Border Fords stood quiet at last, though every watchman knew the real rot lay deeper south where the river spilled into Redmarsh.

title: Embers Over the Black Peat
text: After the false lanterns went dark and the Mire-Cult altars lay shattered in the silt, peat-cutters returned cautiously to the raised boardwalks of Redmarsh. Quicklime trenches were sealed and drained, though green marsh-gas still bubbled through the reeds whenever thunder rolled across the dikes. Without tax-wagons or royal garrisons to enforce old decrees, the surviving apothecaries and ferrymen forged their own rough truce, trading bitter-root salves for dry grain from the north. Behind you, the bog slowly swallowed the ruins, leaving only bleached cairns above the black water.

title: Salt and Quiet Tides
text: Once the corsair blockades shattered against the reefs and the false wreckers' cranes were toppled into the surf, Ironcamp's harbor chain was winched down for the first time in three winters. Surviving fishermen mended tarred nets along the piers while lighthouse keepers relit the cliff-beacons with salvaged whale-oil. Though barnacle-scarred hulls still jutted from the southern coves like broken ribs, honest merchant skiffs dared the coastal currents again—carrying grim rumors of smoke darkening the sky above the inland capital.

title: Cold Dust on the Throne
text: When the foundry furnaces cooled and the last brazier along the Cinder Causeway guttered out, gray ash settled over an empty marble throne. In Oakhaven, clerks and blacksmiths pulled down the Inquisition's iron cages to forge water-pumps and cistern gates, while refugees swept soot from the blackened orchards in hopes that spring rain might coax green shoots from the roots. No new king claimed the scorched crown; instead, the surviving towns bound themselves by a plain ledger of mutual defense, leaving the capital's melted bells to ring only in the wind.
